opus-5.5.text:
Well, the connection really goes back to the work by Yarin Gal and Zoubin Ghahramani, who showed that if you leave dropout turned on at test time, so-called Monte Carlo dropout, you can interpret the network as approximately performing variational Bayesian inference. Each time you run a forward pass with a different random dropout mask, you're effectively sampling a different network from an approximate posterior distribution over the weights. If you do that many times and look at the spread of the predictions, the variance across those samples is supposed to reflect epistemic uncertainty, the uncertainty that comes from our limited knowledge of the right model, as opposed to aleatoric uncertainty, which is the irreducible noise in the data itself.

I think that's a lovely idea, and it's cheap, which is why it caught on. But I've become somewhat skeptical about how well it actually captures epistemic uncertainty in practice. The variational family implied by dropout is quite restricted, and the amount of variation you get depends heavily on the dropout rate, which is a hyperparameter you choose, not something the data tells you. So the "posterior" can be badly miscalibrated. In a lot of empirical comparisons, deep ensembles, where you train several networks from different random initializations, tend to give better uncertainty estimates, and those aren't Bayesian in any strict sense.

There's also a deeper issue that I care about a lot, coming from the open-world and anomaly detection side. Epistemic uncertainty in the Bayesian sense is uncertainty about which model in your hypothesis space is correct, given the training distribution. It doesn't necessarily tell you that a test input is something completely novel, an object from a category you never saw. A network can be confidently wrong on out-of-distribution inputs, and all the dropout samples can agree with each other, because the features it learned simply don't represent the novelty. So I'd say dropout gives you one useful signal of model uncertainty, but we shouldn't mistake it for a complete solution to knowing when the system doesn't know. For that, we need to combine it with methods that explicitly reason about whether the input looks like the training data at all.

r001.rationale: It says Monte Carlo dropout approximately performs variational Bayesian inference, with each dropout mask sampling a network from an approximate posterior over weights.

r002.rationale: It states that the spread or variance across stochastic dropout predictions reflects epistemic uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the connection is interesting, and also a little bit tenuous in some ways. So let me try to unpack it.

Dropout was originally introduced as a regularization technique. During training you randomly zero out some fraction of the hidden units, and that prevents the network from relying too heavily on any particular co-adaptation of features. At test time you turn it off, rescale the weights, and you get a single deterministic prediction. That was the original story, and it had nothing to do with uncertainty per se.

The connection to epistemic uncertainty came from Yarin Gal and Zoubin Ghahramani's work, where they showed that if you keep dropout turned on at test time and you run the network many times with different random masks, you can interpret that as approximately sampling from a posterior distribution over the network's weights. Each dropout mask corresponds to a slightly different network, so you're effectively getting an ensemble, and the variance across those predictions can be read as a measure of the model's uncertainty about the function it has learned. That's the epistemic piece, uncertainty due to limited data and limited knowledge, as opposed to aleatoric uncertainty, which is the inherent noise in the outcome that no amount of data will remove.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the theoretical justification rests on a particular variational approximation, and it's a pretty crude one. The approximate posterior is a mixture of two delta functions for each weight, so to speak, the weight is either present or it's zero. That's a very restricted family, and in practice what you observe is that the uncertainty estimates you get from Monte Carlo dropout tend to be underdispersed. The model is more confident than it should be, particularly on inputs that are far from the training distribution, which is precisely the regime where you most want epistemic uncertainty to be large.

So my own view is that Monte Carlo dropout is best understood as a cheap approximation to an ensemble. If you compare it empirically to deep ensembles, where you train several independent networks from different random initializations, the ensembles almost always give you better calibrated uncertainty and better out-of-distribution detection. The dropout masks don't explore the weight space nearly as widely as independent training runs do, because all of the sampled networks share the same underlying trained weights. You're sampling in a small neighborhood around one mode of the loss surface.

That said, it has the enormous practical advantage that it costs you nothing extra at training time. You've already trained with dropout, and now you get an uncertainty estimate for the price of a few extra forward passes. So in settings where you can't afford to train five or ten models, it's a reasonable thing to do, as long as you understand its limitations. I'd treat it as a signal that something might be off, rather than as a well-calibrated probability you'd want to make high-stakes decisions on.

And the deeper issue, which I think the field is still wrestling with, is that none of these methods really capture what I'd call the open-category problem. If the test input is something the network has never seen anything like, the hidden representation can land in an arbitrary place, and neither the dropout variance nor the ensemble disagreement is guaranteed to be large there. So I see dropout-based uncertainty as one useful tool, but I'd be reluctant to say it solves the epistemic uncertainty problem in any fundamental sense.

r001.rationale: It says that keeping dropout active at test time and sampling different masks approximates sampling from a posterior distribution over the weights.

r002.rationale: It states that variance across the resulting predictions measures the model’s uncertainty, identifying this as epistemic uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
Well, epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty that comes from not knowing which model is right, given the data that we have. In a Bayesian approach, we would maintain a posterior distribution over models and average their predictions. If those models disagree, that gives us an indication of epistemic uncertainty.

Dropout gives us an approximate way of doing something like that. Normally, we use dropout during training and turn it off when we make predictions. But if we leave it on at prediction time and run the same input through the network repeatedly, each random dropout mask gives us a somewhat different prediction. We can average those predictions and look at their variability.

There’s a theoretical connection between that procedure and approximate Bayesian inference. But the qualification is important: these aren’t exact samples from the full posterior over neural networks. So I would think of it as a computationally convenient approximation, rather than a guarantee that we’ve captured all the uncertainty. In particular, if we encounter something very different from the training data, those predictions might still agree and be confidently wrong.

r001.rationale: It describes leaving dropout active at prediction time so random masks produce different predictions, and calls this a computationally convenient approximation with a theoretical connection to Bayesian inference.

r002.rationale: It says to examine the variability among repeated stochastic-dropout predictions as an indication of epistemic uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty about the model that arises because we have limited training data. There may be several models that explain the observations equally well but make different predictions on a new example.

Dropout gives us a way to approximate that idea. During training, we randomly drop out units, so we’re effectively training a collection of networks that share weights. Normally, at prediction time, we turn dropout off. But if we leave it on and run the same input through the network multiple times, we get different predictions from different dropout masks. The variation among those predictions gives us an estimate of epistemic uncertainty.

There’s a Bayesian interpretation of this as an approximate posterior over models. But I’d emphasize the word approximate. These networks share weights, and the distribution of models you get is constrained by the dropout procedure. So it’s a useful, relatively inexpensive technique, but we shouldn’t assume that agreement among those predictions means the model is certain in a well-calibrated sense—particularly on inputs very different from the training data.

r001.rationale: It describes leaving dropout on at prediction time and says this has a Bayesian interpretation as an approximate posterior over models.

r002.rationale: It states that variation across predictions from different dropout masks estimates epistemic uncertainty.
